title: Family: the endings that mean "my" and "your"
goal: Name family members, attach possessive endings to nouns, and see how Uzbek says "my" and "your" with a short ending on the noun itself.
bekal: name the members of the immediate family and tell older from younger siblings — which is required in Uzbek
ask *Nechta aka-ukangiz bor?* and answer it

dialogs.title: Dialog — Oila surati
dialogs.intro: In the university cafeteria. Budi takes out his phone and shows Nilufar a photo of his family.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bu mening oilam. Bu otam, bu esa onam.
lines.id: This is my family. This is my father, and this is my mother.
lines.literal: this my family-my. this father-my, this as-for mother-my.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: He's a doctor. And my mother is a teacher.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: How many brothers do you have?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bitta akam va bitta ukam bor. Singlim ham bor.
lines.id: I have one older brother and one younger brother. I also have a younger sister.
lines.literal: one older-brother-my and one younger-brother-my there-are. younger-sister-my also there-is.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: How old is your younger sister?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: U oʻn olti yoshda. Sizning oilangiz katta?
lines.id: She's sixteen. Is your family big?
lines.literal: she ten six age-at. your family-your big?

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Ha, juda katta. Bizning oilamiz oʻn kishi.
lines.id: Yes, very big. There are ten of us in our family.
lines.literal: yes, very big. our family-our ten person.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Voy! Bobongiz va buvingiz ham birgami?
lines.id: Wow! Do your grandfather and grandmother live with you too?
lines.literal: wow! grandfather-your and grandmother-your also together-?

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.id: Of course. In Uzbekistan that's normal.

notes: **Aka-uka is one word.** Uzbek joins two opposite words into one umbrella term: *aka-uka* (brothers), *opa-singil* (sisters), *ota-ona* (parents), *er-xotin* (husband and wife). English does something similar with "brothers and sisters" — Uzbek just glues the pair together.

**Older and younger must be distinguished.** *Aka* (older brother) and *uka* (younger brother) are two different words; so are *opa* and *singil*. English has no such distinction, so get into the habit of asking yourself "older or younger?" every time you say "brother" or "sister".

**Necha yoshda? literally "at what age?".** Age is expressed with the locative ending *-da*: *oʻn olti yoshda* = "at sixteen years". Uzbek doesn't say "has sixteen years" like French, nor "is sixteen" like English.

**Nechta asks "how many (items)", necha asks "how many/what" in general.** *Nechta kitob?* (how many books), but *necha yoshda?* (how old) and *soat necha?* (what time is it). The difference is subtle; learn those two common phrases as they are.
**Bitta = "one (item)".** The number *bir* plus *-ta* gives the form used when counting things: *bitta*, *ikkita*, *uchta*. The whole system comes in unit 5.

grammars.title: Possessive endings — six forms, one simple idea
body: Where English puts "my" or "your" in front of a noun, Uzbek attaches an ending to the noun itself: "my friend" is *doʻstim*. Once you have that idea, all that's left is to learn the six endings.
after: The rule fits in one sentence: **if the word ends in a consonant, insert *i*; if it ends in a vowel, attach directly.** *kitob* → *kitobim*, but *ona* → *onam*. In the third person, a vowel needs an *s*: *ona* → *ona**s**i*.

⚠️ **Some words drop their last vowel** when an ending is added: *singil* → *singlim*, *oʻgʻil* → *oʻgʻlim*, *ogʻiz* (mouth) → *ogʻzim*, *burun* (nose) → *burnim*, *shahar* (city) → *shahrim*. The list is short and they're all very common words, so they stick on their own.
⚠️ **The letters k and q soften** before an ending that starts with a vowel: *yurak* (heart) → *yura**g**im*, *qishloq* (village) → *qishlo**gʻ**im*. The same pattern comes back in units 7 and 8.

grammars.title: Mening kitobim — two markers for one owner
body: Uzbek can name the owner in front **and** attach the ending at the back. It sounds like overkill; it's actually very useful.
after: **The ending at the back is required; the pronoun in front can be dropped.** *Kitobim* already means "my book". Use the pronoun when you want to stress the owner: *Mening kitobim* = "**my** book, not yours".

The reverse doesn't work: *mening kitob* is **wrong**. If the owner is named, the ending must still be there. This is beginners' mistake number one, and the only cure is to say both parts as one package from today on.
To answer "whose?" without naming the thing, use *-niki*: *Bu kitob kimniki?* — *Meniki.* (Whose book is this? — Mine.)

blocks.text: Notice that almost all of them are native Turkic words, not loans — a sign that family words are the oldest layer of a language.

⚠️ *Aka* and *opa* aren't just family words. Both are used as **respectful forms of address for strangers a little older than you**: a waiter, a taxi driver, a seller at the bozor. *Rahmat, aka!* to a man, *Rahmat, opa!* to a woman. Using them makes you sound like someone who knows the customs.
Uzbek first names often get *-jon* as a sign of affection: *Nilufarjon*, *Budijon*. It comes from the Persian word *jon* (soul, life) — think of it as "dear".
One question you're sure to hear within five minutes of meeting anyone.

Notice the ending **-chi**: it turns a noun into "the person who deals with it", much like English *-er*. *Ish* (work) → *ishchi* (worker), *sot-* (to sell) → *sotuvchi*, *dastur* (program) → *dasturchi*. Once you see the pattern, you can guess dozens of job names without learning them.

The sentences are simple because they need no verb at all: *Men dasturchiman* (I'm a programmer), *U shifokor* (He/She is a doctor), *Siz oʻqituvchimisiz?* (Are you a teacher?). Everything from unit 1 is put to use right away.
